title: Income Tax (Managed Investment Trust Withholding Tax) Amendment Bill 2018
short_title: Income Tax (Managed Investment Trust Withholding Tax) Amendment Bill 2018

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill is part of a package that tightens tax rules for foreign investors using stapled structures and limits their access to concessions.
It would amend the Income Tax (Managed Investment Trust Withholding Tax) Act 2008 to set the withholding rate on non-concessional managed investment trust income at 30 per cent.
The explanatory memorandum also says the package would amend the Income Tax Rates Act 1986 to make sovereign entities liable to income tax at 30 per cent.
changes: Sets the managed investment trust withholding rate on non-concessional income at 30 per cent.
Makes consequential amendments to the Income Tax (Managed Investment Trust Withholding Tax) Act 2008.
Amends the Income Tax Rates Act 1986 to apply a 30 per cent income tax rate to sovereign entities.
summary.affected: Foreign investors using stapled structures and sovereign entities.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: The government opposed suspending standing orders, citing important business including the bipartisan passage of strawberry industry legislation, and listed several bills for introduction, such as the Higher Education Support Amendment (VET FEE-HELP Student Protection) Bill 2018 and the Treasury Laws Amendment (Making Sure Foreign Investors Pay Their Fair Share of Tax in Australia and Other Measures) Bill 2018.

speeches.speaker: Tim Wilson
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that Labor’s policy to remove refundable franking credits would effectively impose a "retirement tax" on a million Australian retirees, stealing their overpaid tax. He noted the Economics Committee is conducting an inquiry into the issue, not opposition policy, and that affected retirees want comprehensive tax reform rather than targeted changes.

speeches.speaker: Bert van Manen
speeches.brief: The three bills close tax loopholes for foreign investors, particularly stapled structures and double-gearing, which allowed them to pay under 15% tax or nothing on Australian business income while Australian entities pay up to 30%. The measures are expected to raise $400 million over the forward estimates and build on previous actions that have raised about $7 billion in liabilities from multinationals.
